title: AI document processing: which AI reads files with no wrong numbers
description: We benchmarked AI tools on 30 sealed fund reports. Which ones made no mistakes, what each costs per page, and three ways to build it.
summary: AI document processing turns PDFs, scans and forms into fields your systems can use. Reading the text is now cheap. The hard part is knowing which fields came out wrong, on your files rather than a vendor's demo set. We built a benchmark to find out.
verdict: Have a frontier model read the raw PDF, have a second model read it too, and send only the facts they disagree on to a person. In our sealed benchmark of 30 fund reports, the two best models made zero mistakes at $0.12 to $0.15 per report. Don't trust a model's own confidence score: wrong answers came back rated 70 to 100.

pickElse: You process thousands of standard invoices or receipts a day: a cloud prebuilt parser costs about $10 per 1,000 pages at AWS and Azure and handles volume for you.

Your files cannot leave your network: run open-source Docling (MIT licence) or a local model. Expect more wrong values: in our first round the two local models made 8 wrong values each where Claude Haiku 5.5 made none.
You only need searchable text, not fields: basic OCR is about $1.50 per 1,000 pages at all three big clouds.

ownData.title: Our benchmark: 30 fund reports, keys sealed before any AI read them
ownData.intro: FinExtractBench is Zavient's own benchmark. We picked 30 public private-fund reports (781 pages), wrote the correct answer for every fact by hand and locked the answers before any tool ran. A mistake is a wrong value, a value the report never states, or an event it does not support. Each tool read each raw PDF once.
ownData.note: Limits: one person wrote the answers; the reports are digital, in English and at most 56 pages. Zero mistakes in 30 reports still allows a true rate of up to about 1 report in 10. A scan check on 10 of the reports, as page pictures, also found 0 mistakes for both tools. When the two tools disagreed, 66 facts went to a person, about 2 per report.

example.input: A 57-page quarterly report from a private equity fund, as a PDF.
example.output: Committed capital, paid-in capital, distributions, net asset value, DPI and TVPI, each with the page number and the exact words it came from, plus a flag on any fact the two models disagree on.

howToTest: Pick 50 real files, including your worst scans and longest reports. Include facts some files do not state, to catch invented answers.
Write the right answer for every fact before any AI reads the files, and lock it. Answers written after you see the AI's output drift toward it.
Require each answer to name its page and quote the exact words, and have code check that the quote is there.
Count wrong answers apart from blanks. A blank costs a person a minute; a wrong number can cost a deal.
Compare cost and time per file, and run the winner again on new files before you go live.

buyVsBuild.buy: Buy a prebuilt parser or an AP tool when your files are standard invoices, receipts or IDs and you mainly need volume and an audit trail.
buyVsBuild.build: Build on frontier models when your files are specific to your business, the facts feed your own systems, and a wrong number is expensive. The build is small: a prompt, a fact list, a checker and a review queue.

watchOuts: Vendor accuracy numbers come from the vendor's own files. Even on our sealed set, the AI was right and our hand-written answer was wrong in 22 of 57 disputes. Check your answer key too.
A model that writes a plausible wrong number is worse than one that leaves the field blank. Score them separately.
Two tables on one page with similar labels fooled 7 of 10 tools in our hard round. Check the facts that sit near look-alikes.
Prices and model versions change every few weeks. Re-run your benchmark when either changes, and keep the files and answers so the re-run is cheap.
Read the vendor's data terms. Datalab's pricing page shows a 25% discount by default if you let it keep your data.

rules.name: EU AI Act, Annex III
rules.what: Reading documents is not a high-risk use on its own. It becomes part of one when the facts feed credit scoring of people or life and health insurance pricing; then logging, human oversight and documentation apply.

rules.name: Regulation B, 12 CFR 1002.9
rules.what: If extracted facts feed a US credit decision, a decline still needs specific reasons. A wrongly read fact becomes a wrong reason, so keep the page and quote behind every fact.

rules.name: NYDFS Circular Letter No. 7
rules.what: New York insurers stay responsible for vendor AI tools, including extraction, and need audit rights in the contract.
